claims.text: The extent of atomic-size-mismatch-induced lattice distortion controls phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
Greater lattice distortion favors a disordered solid solution over ordered intermetallic phases.
Retention of a disordered solid solution underpins high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
The initial near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy can be homogeneous and single-phase disordered.
Changing Al content can systematically change the degree of lattice distortion.
Substituting an element with one of a different atomic radius can systematically change lattice distortion.
Atomic size mismatch produces local strain fields.
Local strain fields caused by enhanced atomic size mismatch hinder formation of ordered intermetallic phases.
Suppression of ordered intermetallic formation promotes a disordered solid solution.
A disordered solid solution effectively accommodates defects and stress.
An optimal level of lattice distortion will stabilize the disordered phase relative to a less-distorted baseline.
An optimally distorted alloy will have superior high-temperature mechanical strength relative to the baseline.
An optimally distorted alloy will have superior environmental resistance relative to the baseline.
An optimally distorted alloy will have improved radiation tolerance relative to the baseline.
An optimally distorted alloy will maintain cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline.
The hypothesis is restricted to alloys processed under near-equilibrium conditions where conventional thermodynamic and kinetic factors govern phase formation.
The proposed mechanism may not apply under extreme non-equilibrium processing or when secondary-phase precipitation dominates behavior.
Direct experimental evidence linking quantified lattice distortion to the full suite of targeted properties in these alloys is absent.

contradictions.description: The prediction invokes an unspecified optimal level of distortion, whereas the falsification rule treats a lack of consistent improvement with increased mismatch as disconfirming. Failure at non-optimal mismatch levels would not falsify the existence of an optimum.
